summary: The note describes how Cubism influenced fields beyond painting and sculpture, especially literature, through Gertrude Stein's use of repetition. It also covers the 1912 book Du "Cubisme" by Jean Metzinger and Albert Gleizes and some of the works shown in the early Cubist exhibitions.
one_line: Covers Cubism's influence on literature through Gertrude Stein, and the 1912 treatise Du "Cubisme" with works from early Cubist exhibitions.
key_facts: The influence of Cubism extended to fields outside painting and sculpture, including literature.
Gertrude Stein's written works use repetition and repetitive phrases as building blocks in both passages and whole chapters.
Most of Gertrude Stein's important works use this repetition technique, including the novel The Making of Americans (1906–08).
Gertrude Stein and her brother Leo were the first important patrons of Cubism.
Gertrude Stein and her brother Leo were also important influences on Cubism.
Picasso was an important influence on Stein's writing.
Jean Metzinger and Albert Gleizes wrote Du "Cubisme".
Du "Cubisme" was published by Eugène Figuière in 1912 and translated to English and Russian in 1913.
Du "Cubisme" was written against a background of public anger.
Le Fauconnier's vast composition Les Montagnards attaqués par des ours (Mountaineers Attacked by Bears) is now at the Rhode Island School of Design Museum.
Joseph Csaky's sculpture Deux Femme (Two Women) is now lost.
Kupka's highly abstract painting Amorpha is held by The National Gallery, Prague.
Picabia's painting La Source (The Spring) is held by the Museum of Modern Art, New York.
